inline.s: [Juzhi raised a finger] The monk Juzhi (
zhī

), when he had just taken up residence in his hut, was visited by a nun named Shiji. She wore a bamboo hat, carried a staff, and circled the master three times, saying, “If you can say it, I will take off my hat.” She asked this three times, and each time the master had no reply, so the nun left. The master said, “The sun is getting late; why not stay for a while?” The nun said, “If you can say it, I will stay.” Again the master had no reply. After the nun had gone, the master sighed, “Though I have a man's body, I have no man's spirit. I would rather abandon this hut and travel about seeking good and wise teachers.” That night the mountain spirit told him, “There is no need to leave this place; a bodhisattva in flesh will soon come to teach the Dharma to the master.” After more than ten days, sure enough, the monk Tianlong arrived at the hut. The master at once came out to greet and bow to him and told him the whole matter. Tianlong raised one finger and showed it to him, and the master was instantly greatly enlightened. From then on, whenever a student came to ask about anything, the master would simply raise one finger and give no other exposition. There was a young boy who, whenever he saw people ask about anything, also raised his finger. People said to the master, “Master, the boy also understands the Dharma; whenever asked, he raises his finger just as you do.” One day the master concealed a knife in his sleeve and asked the boy, “I hear you understand the Dharma, is that so?” The boy said, “It is so.” The master said, “What is the Buddha?” The boy raised his finger, and the master cut it off with the knife. The boy cried out and ran away. The master called the boy; the boy turned his head. The master said, “What is the Buddha?” The boy raised his hand and, seeing no finger, was suddenly greatly enlightened. When the master was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, “I obtained the one-finger Chan of Tianlong, and in a whole life I did not use it up.” Having said this, he entered extinction. [Tipiao] Also written as tichang or tigang, meaning to raise up and sing the essentials. That is, the way the Chan grove takes up and sets forth the essentials of the school to students. Generally one sings out the essential words of the ancients, so it is also called niangu (picking out the old) or niannong (handling the old). This is because the purpose of the Chan school is a special transmission outside the teaching, not relying on written words; therefore, although one speaks the recorded sayings, one only points to the essentials of the school, and students who wish to understand this matter must diligently study and investigate. Other schools call this jiangshi (explaining) or jiangyi (expounding the meaning).
[The earth-striking monk of Xin (
xīn

) Prefecture] A monk of Xin Prefecture, after he had awakened under Master Mazu, hid his name. Whenever a student came to seek instruction, he would only strike the ground with a stick to show him. Everyone called him the earth-striking master. In “the earth-striking one of Xin Prefecture,” the “Xin Prefecture” is an honorific usage of old times in which a person is named by his place; here it stands for the earth-striking master. [Yunyan's lion] Chan Master Yaoshan asked Chan Master Yunyan, “I hear you are very good at dancing the lion, is that so?” Chan Master Yunyan said, “It is so.” Yaoshan said, “How many acts can you dance?” Yunyan said, “I can dance six acts.” Yaoshan said, “I too can dance the lion.” Yunyan said, “How many acts can you, Master, dance?” Yaoshan said, “I dance one act.” Yunyan said, “The one is the six, the six is the one.” After Yunyan had been awakened and realized his understanding, he once came to visit Chan Master Weishan. Weishan asked, “I hear that you danced the lion at Yaoshan's place, is that so?” Yunyan said, “It is so.” Weishan asked, “Do you dance continuously, or is there a time when you stop?” Yunyan said, “When I want to dance, I dance; when I want to stop, I stop.” Weishan asked, “When you stop, where is the lion?” Yunyan said, “Stop, stop!”

blocks.text: 5. Substance and Function, One and Different

inline.s: (Original title: The substance and function of the true mind, one and different)

[Someone asks: The substance and function of the true mind, I do not know whether they are one or different? Answer: In terms of characteristics they are not one; in terms of nature they are not different. Therefore this substance and function are neither one nor different.]

Question: The substance and function of the true mind, I do not know whether they are one or two? Answer: In terms of characteristics they are two; in terms of nature they are one. Therefore the substance and function of the true mind are neither one nor two.

[How do we know this is so? Let me try to discuss it: The wondrous substance is unmoving, cutting off all duality, apart from all characteristics; only one who has reached and realized the nature can fathom its principle. The wondrous function follows conditions, responding to all the many kinds, falsely establishing empty characteristics, seeming to have shape. By this having characteristics and being without characteristics, they are not one. Again, the function issues from the substance, so the function does not depart from the substance; the substance can put forth the function, so the substance does not depart from the function. By this principle of their not being separated, they are not different.]

How do we know that the substance and function of the true mind are neither one nor two? Let me now explain it for you: The wondrous substance of the true mind is unmoving, cut off from all duality, apart from all characteristics; none but one who has realized the nature and verified it can easily understand this principle. The wondrous function of the true mind follows conditions, responding to the many kinds, falsely establishing empty characteristics, seeming to have shape. By the substance being without characteristics and the function having characteristics, the substance and function of the true mind are not one. Again, the function issues from the substance, so the function does not depart from the substance; the substance can put forth the function, so the substance does not depart from the function. By this principle of the substance and characteristics not being separated, the substance and function of the true mind are not two.

[Just as water takes wetness as its substance, and because the substance is unmoving, the wave takes movement as its characteristic, arising because of the wind. The water's nature is unmoving while the wave's characteristic moves, so they are not one. Yet outside the waves there is no water, and outside the water there are no waves; their wetness is one, so they are not different. By analogy, the one and different of substance and function can be understood.]

For example, water takes its wet nature as its substance, and this substance is unmoving; the wave takes movement as its characteristic, arising because of the wind. The water's nature is unmoving while the wave's characteristic moves, so they are not one. Yet outside the waves there is no water, and outside the water there are no waves; their wetness is one and the same, so they are not two. As described above, the principle of the one and different of the substance and function of the true mind becomes clear.

[Someone asks: The substance and function of the true mind are possessed by everyone; why is it that sages and ordinary people differ? Answer: The true mind of sages and ordinary people is originally the same. Ordinary people, with their deluded mind, grasp at objects, and losing their own pure nature, are cut off by this, so the true mind cannot appear before them. It is but like the shadow of a tree in the dark, or a spring underground, present yet unrecognized.]

Question: The substance and function of the true mind are possessed by everyone; how is it that sages and ordinary people are entirely different? Answer: The true mind of sages and ordinary people is originally the same. But ordinary people, with the deluded mind, cling to the dusty realms (the deluded mind grasping at objects), lose their own pure nature, and being cut off by this, the true mind cannot appear before them. At this time the true mind is like the shadow of a tree in the dark, or a spring underground, present but hidden and not appearing.

[Therefore the sutra says: “Good man, just as a pure mani jewel reflects the five colors, each appearing in accordance with the direction, the foolish see the mani jewel as truly having the five colors. Good man, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment appears in body and mind, responding to each class in its own way; the foolish say that the pure perfect enlightenment truly has such self-characteristics of body and mind. It is the same as well.”]

Therefore the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Good man, just as a pure mani jewel reflects the five colors, each appearing in accordance with the direction, the foolish falsely see the mani jewel as truly having the five colors. Good man, the pure nature of perfect enlightenment appears in body and mind, responding to each class in its own way; the foolish erroneously take the pure perfect enlightenment as truly having such self-characteristics of body and mind. It is likewise.”

[The Zhao Treatise says: “Within heaven and earth, between the cosmos, there is a single jewel, hidden in the form-mountain.” This is the true mind wrapped in defilement. Again, Ci'en says: “The Dharma body is originally present, common to all the Buddhas. Ordinary people, covered by delusion, have it yet do not realize it; wrapped in afflictions, it receives the name of the tathagatagarbha.” Sir Pei says: “One who is roundly enlightened all day long yet never roundly enlightened is an ordinary person.” Therefore we know that although the true mind is in the midst of worldly toil, it is not stained by worldly toil; like a white jade cast into mud, its color does not change.]

The Zhao Treatise says: “Within heaven and earth (the cosmos), between the universe, there is a single jewel (the true mind), hidden in the form-mountain (secretly buried in the physical body).” This is the true mind wrapped in defilement. Again, Master Kuiji says: “The Dharma body is originally present, common to all the Buddhas of the three times. Yet ordinary people, covered by delusion, have it yet do not realize it; wrapped in afflictions, it receives the name of the tathagatagarbha.” Pei Xiu says: “One who is roundly enlightened all day long yet never roundly enlightened is an ordinary person.” Therefore we know that although the true mind is in the midst of worldly toil, it is not stained by worldly toil, just as a white jade cast into mud, its pure white color does not change.
[The Zhao Treatise] It is a collection of the treatises written by the monk Sengzhao (
zhào

) of the Later Qin, and the whole book is divided into five parts: the Essence of the Ancestral Teaching, the Treatise on the Non-Movement of Things, the Treatise on the Non-True Emptiness, the Treatise on Prajna as Non-Knowing, and the Treatise on the Unnameable Nirvana; at the end are appended Liu Yimin's letter of inquiry and the reply to Liu Yimin. Sengzhao was one of the most outstanding and influential disciples under Master Kumarajiva, and among the disciples the youngest and most talented. [Tathagatagarbha] The natural state of one's intrinsic nature is called the tathagatagarbha. (For details see
Mind, Intrinsic Nature, and the Tathagatagarbha

[Kuiji] The founding patriarch of the Consciousness-Only school. Because he lived in the Great Kindness and Compassion Monastery of the capital, he was called “Master Ci'en.” He was the only son of the early Tang meritorious minister Yuchi Gong, of an intelligent nature and a majestic physique. At seventeen he was commanded to go forth as a monk, becoming a high disciple of Master Xuanzang, studying Buddhist scriptures and treatises and Indian languages under him; at twenty-five he took part in translating the scriptures. In the fourth year of the Xianqing era of Emperor Gaozong (the year 159), when Master Xuanzang translated the treatise On the Completion of Consciousness-Only and other works, Kuiji alone served as the amanuensis, producing the ten scrolls of the On the Completion of Consciousness-Only, one scroll of the Verse of the Treatise on Discerning the Middle and the Extremes, three scrolls of the Treatise on Discerning the Middle and the Extremes, one scroll of the Twenty Verses on Consciousness-Only, one scroll of the Treatise on the Doctrines of the Different Schools, and three scrolls of the Treatise on the Elements of Body and Base of the Abhidharma. Thereafter Master Xuanzang further expounded to Kuiji Dignaga's Gate of Correct Reasoning and the Treatise on the Yogacara Ground and other treatises. Thus Kuiji penetrated the science of logic and the doctrines of the five natures, and produced vast commentaries, and so was called the master of a hundred commentaries.
Question: What is fundamental ignorance?

Answer: Fundamental ignorance (also called beginningless ignorance) is the first stirring of thought. Because of this single thought rising, the intrinsic nature (the true mind) turns from awareness into delusion, dark and obscured through the long night, not understanding the truth, and giving rise to all the various delusions and afflictions.
Question: “From one thought of non-awareness arise the three subtle marks; with characteristics as the condition grow the six coarse marks.” What does this mean?
Answer: This describes the process of the intrinsic nature passing from awareness into delusion and producing delusion
creating karma
and receiving its retribution. The “three subtle and six coarse marks” are the nine false marks of arising and ceasing, of transmigration
into delusion
illusorily
manifested
by
the intrinsic nature

: the mark of ignorance and karma, the mark of being able to see, the mark of characteristics (the mark of what is seen); the mark of intelligence, the mark of continuity, the mark of grasping, the mark of attaching to names, the mark of producing karma, and the mark of suffering bound by karma.

Of these, the first three arise from fundamental ignorance (“from one thought of non-awareness arise the three subtle marks”); their marks are subtle, so they are called the “three subtle marks.” The latter six grow from the characteristic being the condition (“with characteristics as the condition grow the six coarse marks”); their marks are coarse and manifest, so they are called the “six coarse marks.”
The process is
“The three subtle marks”: First, the mark of ignorance and karma. The mind's movement is karma, so
the unminding mind that moves (the first stirring of thought)
is called the mark of ignorance and karma. Second, the mark of being able to see. Depending upon the foregoing
“mark of ignorance and karma,”
the mind moving, it can see. Third, the mark of characteristics (the mark of what is seen). Depending upon the foregoing “mark of being able to see”
since it can see, characteristics falsely appear.
“The six coarse marks”: First, the mark of intelligence. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of characteristics”
falsely producing the activity of intelligence and discriminating favorable and unfavorable, beautiful and ugly, love and aversion. Second, the mark of continuity. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of intelligence”
discriminating the conditions of objects, thought after thought continuing. Third, the mark of grasping. Depending upon the foregoing “mark of continuity”
turning deeper upon the thoughts of continuity, giving rise to self and what is mine, forming the mark of grasping. Fourth, the mark of attaching to names. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of grasping”
and naming the various states, affairs, and things, forming concepts and language. Fifth, the mark of producing karma. Depending upon the foregoing
mark of attaching to names”
thinking and calculating, producing the various karma of body, speech, and mind. Sixth, the mark of suffering bound by karma. Depending upon the foregoing “mark of producing karma”,
bound by the karma of body, speech, and mind that is produced
it is bound
and experiences the bitter fruit of birth and death.

Question: Sentient beings are originally Buddhas; because of one thought of non-awareness they have ignorance and fall into being sentient beings. If one practices and attains buddhahood, could one again have a thought of non-awareness and ignorance, and fall back into being a sentient being?

Answer: No. Now, when we practice and attain buddhahood, it is precisely to eradicate beginningless ignorance. Therefore, after attaining buddhahood, one will not again have ignorance and fall into being a sentient being. This is like a person who, when he has not yet had smallpox, is a healthy person; having had smallpox, he becomes a sick person; after he recovers, he is again a healthy person and, possessing lifelong immunity, will never have smallpox again. In the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment, the bodhisattva Vajragarbha also asked this question: “Sentient beings of the ten directions originally accomplished the Buddha-way, and afterwards gave rise to ignorance. When will all the Tathagatas again produce all afflictions?” The World-Honored One answered: “Good man! It is like smelting a gold mine; the gold does not exist because of the smelting. Once it has become gold, it will not be turned back into ore.

The perfect enlightenment of the Tathagata is likewise.” (Translation: Good man! As in smelting and refining a gold mine, the gold does not exist because of the smelting; since it has already become pure gold, it will not again become ore.
The perfect enlightenment of the Tathagata is also like this, and does not reverse.)

blocks.text: 7. Stillling the Deluded Mind of the True Mind

inline.s: [Someone asks: The true mind dwelling in delusion, then one is an ordinary person; how can one come out of delusion and become a sage? Answer: The ancients say: “Where the deluded mind is nowhere, that is bodhi; birth and death and nirvana are originally equal.” The sutra says: “That sentient being, his illusory body being extinguished, the illusory mind is also extinguished; the illusory mind being extinguished, the illusory dust is also extinguished; the illusory dust being extinguished, the illusory extinction is also extinguished; the illusory extinction being extinguished, what is not illusory is not extinguished. It is like polishing a mirror; when the dust is gone, the brightness appears.”]

Question: The true mind dwelling in delusion, then one is an ordinary person; how can one come out of delusion and become a sage? Answer: The ancients say: “When there is no deluded mind, that is bodhi; birth and death and nirvana are originally equal.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “That sentient being (the one who practices the contemplation of extinguishing illusion), in his contemplation, his illusory body being extinguished, the illusory mind (the illusory consciousness) is extinguished; the illusory mind being extinguished, the illusory dust (the world) is extinguished; the illusory dust (the world) being extinguished, the contemplation that extinguishes illusion also is extinguished (the illusory extinction likewise extinguished; this is getting the fish and forgetting the trap, casting off layer after layer); the contemplation being extinguished, there remains only the pure perfect-enlightenment mind, not of the same as the illusory, which is not extinguished, like polishing a mirror; when the dust is gone, the brightness appears.”

[Bodhi] Translated into Chinese as “awakening,” it refers to the wisdom that can know the Dharma-nature, that is, the great wisdom that exhausts all afflictions. [Getting the fish and forgetting the trap (
quán

)] The trap, also written “quan,” is a bamboo implement for catching fish. It means that once the fish is caught, one forgets the implement. It is a metaphor for, once success is attained, forgetting what one relied upon; or, once the goal is reached, setting aside the means and method. [Birth and death and nirvana are originally equal] The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Perfect enlightenment universally shines; quiescence and extinction are non-dual. Amid it, the hundreds of thousands of millions of asamkhyeyas of inexpressible Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are like flowers in empty space, arising and ceasing in confusion. Neither identical with nor apart from, neither bound nor released, then one knows that sentient beings are originally Buddhas, and that birth and death and nirvana are like a dream of last night.” (For the commentary, see
The Detailed Explanation of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment

[Yongjia also says: “The mind is the root, the dharmas are the dust; the two are like the traces upon a mirror. When the traces and dust are gone, the light appears; when mind and dharma are both forgotten, the nature is true.” This is coming out of delusion and becoming true.]

Master Yongjia's Song of Realizing the Way also says: “The consciousness-mind is the six faculties (of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind); the various dharmas are the six objects (forms, sounds, scents, tastes, tangible objects, and mental objects). These two (the consciousness-mind and the dharmas) are like the traces upon the mirror (the mind-essence); when the traces and dust are gone the mirror's light appears, and when mind and dharma are both extinguished (the faculties and objects fall away) it becomes the state of the true mind.” This is what is meant by the true mind coming out of delusion and becoming true (the return from delusion to the state of awareness).

[When mind and dharma are both forgotten, the nature is true] With the consciousness-mind and the various dharmas both extinguished, one returns to the state of awareness of the true mind. In classical texts, “wang” is used for “wang” (to extinguish).
[Someone asks: Master Zhuang says: “The mind, when hot, scorches
(used for “scorched”)

like fire; when cold, congeals like ice; so swift that in the twinkling of an eye it again roams beyond the four seas; when still, deep and quiet; when moving, hanging aloft in the sky, this is only the human mind!” This is Master Zhuang first speaking of how the ordinary person's mind is hard to subdue. I do not know by what method the school treats the deluded mind? Answer: By the method of no-mind it treats the deluded mind.]

Question: Master Zhuang says: “The mind, in its fierceness, is hot like a blazing fire; in its decline, cold like a bitter frost; so swift that in the twinkling of an eye it can again wander beyond the four seas; when at rest, deep and serene; when moving, leaping up to the high heavens, I fear only the human mind can do this!” This is the late Master Zhuang first speaking of how the ordinary person's mind is so hard to subdue. I do not know by what method the school treats the deluded mind? Answer: By the method of no-mind one treats the deluded mind.

[The twinkling of an eye] The time of a single lowering and raising of the head. It describes an extremely short time. [Deluded mind] The true mind dwelling in a state of delusion (the true mind in delusion) is called the deluded mind.

[Someone asks: If a person has no mind, he is the same as plants and trees; the saying of no-mind, please give the expedient means. Answer: What I call no-mind does not mean being without the mind-essence, called no-mind. It is only that in the mind there is nothing, and this is called no-mind. For example, an empty bottle is called an empty bottle because there is nothing in the bottle, not because the bottle's substance does not exist. Therefore the patriarch says: “You have only to have no affairs in the mind, and no mind in the affairs; then naturally it is empty and spiritual, still and wondrous.” This is the purport of this mind. According to this, the point is to have no deluded mind, not to be without the wondrous function of the true mind.]

Question: If a person has no mind, he is the same as plants and trees; the saying of no-mind, please analyze it in detail for me. Answer: What I call no-mind does not mean that being without the mind-essence is called no-mind. It is only that in the mind there is nothing, and this is called no-mind. For example, when one speaks of an empty bottle, it is called an empty bottle because there is nothing in the bottle; it is not called an empty bottle because the bottle's substance does not exist. Therefore the patriarch says: “You have only to have no affairs in the mind, and no mind in the affairs; then the mind-essence naturally is empty and spiritual, still and wondrous.” This is the essential purport of stilling the deluded mind of the true mind. According to this, stilling the deluded mind of the true mind takes having no deluded mind as its essential purport; it does not mean being without the wondrous function of the true mind.

The Essentials of the Dharma of Mind-Transmission says: “Therefore, the student of the Way, only recognizing seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and the functioning of action, if he empties out seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, then the path of the mind is cut off, and there is no place to enter; he has but to recognize the original mind at the place of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. Yet the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, nor does it depart from seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. Only, do not form views upon seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing; do not move the thought upon them; do not seek the mind apart from them; and do not reject seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing to grasp the dharma. Neither identical with nor apart, neither abiding nor attached, free everywhere at will, there is nowhere that is not the way-place.”

It also says: “Therefore, the student of the Way, deluded about his own original mind, does not recognize it as the Buddha, and so seeks outside, engaging in the practice of functions, making progress by stages, toiling through countless kalpas, and never accomplishing the Way. It is preferable to be without mind in the present moment, with certainty knowing that all dharmas are originally without any possession and also without any attainment, without reliance and without abiding, without subject and without object, without moving a false thought, and then verify bodhi. When one verifies the Way, one verifies only the original-mind Buddha; the toil of kalpas is all empty cultivation. Like the warrior who obtains the jewel, he obtains only the original jewel on his forehead, having nothing to do with the effort of seeking outside.”

[The jewel on the forehead] Using the jewel on the forehead as a metaphor for the Buddha-nature (the true mind) originally possessed by everyone. The Nirvana Sutra gives this parable: a warrior wrestling with another, their heads colliding, the diamond jewel between his brows sank into his skin, and a sore grew there. Later a good physician told him of it, and only then did he know the diamond jewel had entered his body. This is a metaphor for how all sentient beings, because covered by afflictions, do not know the Buddha-nature they originally possess; once they encounter a good and wise teacher, only then do they come to see the Buddha-nature they originally possess.
[From of old, the various masters' methods of practicing the no-mind work have each been different; now summarizing their great meaning, I briefly indicate ten kinds:]

The methods of practicing the no-mind work spoken of by the various patriarchs of the past, by category, are each different; now I will gather them together as ten kinds and briefly explain them as follows:

[The first is called awareness. It means that when doing the work, ordinarily one is without thought, guarding against the rising of thoughts. The moment a thought arises, one immediately breaks it with awareness. When the false thought is broken by awareness, the following thought does not arise. When the work is mature, this awareness-wisdom is also not needed, and both delusion and awareness are forgotten. This is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: “Do not fear that thoughts arise; only fear that awareness is slow.” And a verse says: “Do not seek truth; only be still your views.” This is the work of stilling delusion.]

The first is awareness. When doing the work, ordinarily one is in the state of no-thought (ordinarily without thought), guarding against the rising of thoughts at all times. The moment a thought arises, one immediately breaks it with awareness; when the false thought is broken, the following thought does not arise. When the work is mature, this awareness-wisdom is also not needed, and both false thoughts and awareness are extinguished. This is called no-mind. Therefore the patriarch says: “Do not fear that thoughts arise; only fear that awareness is slow.” He also says: “You need not seek the true mind; only still the arising of thought (be still your views), and the true mind naturally appears.” This is the work of stilling false thoughts.

[The second is called resting. It means that when doing the work, one thinks neither of good nor of evil; when a thought arises, one rests it; when a condition is met, one rests. The ancients say: “Go like a single bolt of white silk, go cold and forlorn; in the old temple, go like the incense burner.” When one reaches the point of cutting off all subtle activity and separation, free of discrimination, like a dullard or a blockhead, then there is a little corresponding. This is the work of resting the deluded mind.]

The second is called resting. When doing the work, one thinks neither of good nor of evil; when a thought arises, one rests it (does not continue it); when a condition is met, one rests (does not cling). The Chan Master Shishuang (Qingzhu of the Tang dynasty) says: “Go like a single bolt of white silk, go cold and forlorn; in the old temple, go like the incense burner.” Until one has extinguished the subtle rising of thought and freed oneself from all the false views of clinging discrimination, like a dullard or a blockhead, only then is there a little correspondence. This is the work of resting false thoughts.

[A single bolt of white silk] White silk: white silk cloth. Here the white silk is a metaphor for the mind-thought being pure and unmixed, the state of the ten thousand thoughts converging into one. “Go like a single bolt of white silk” means to take away even that single thought (the one returning to nothing), and enter the state of no-thought. [In the old temple, go like the incense burner] The incense burner of the old temple (the single wisp of incense-fire remaining in the old temple): a metaphor for the mind-thought being pure and unmixed, the state of the ten thousand thoughts converging into one. “Go like the old temple incense burner” (taking away even the single wisp of incense-fire remaining in the old temple) is also a metaphor for the one returning to nothing and entering the state of no-thought. [Subtle activity] Fine and small.

blocks.text: 3. Extinguishing the Mind and Preserving the Realm

inline.s: [Third, extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm. It means that when doing the work, all false thoughts are extinguished. Paying no regard to the external realm, one has only to still one's own mind. The false mind being already stilled, what harm is there in having a realm? This is the ancients' approach of seizing the person and not the realm. Hence there is the saying: “Everywhere there is fragrant grass; the whole city is without an old friend.” And the layman Pang says: “Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things; what harm that the ten thousand things surround you?” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm.]

Third, extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm. When doing the work, all false thoughts are extinguished. Paying no attention to the external realm, one has only to still one's own mind. Because the false mind is already stilled, what harm is there in a realm? This is the ancients' approach of seizing the mind and not the realm. Hence the verse says: “Everywhere there is fragrant grass (the realm); the whole city is without an old friend (the mind).” And the layman Pang says: “Only be without mind toward the ten thousand things; what harm that the ten thousand things perpetually surround you?” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and preserving the realm.

blocks.text: 4. Extinguishing the Realm and Preserving the Mind

inline.s: [Fourth, extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind. It means that when doing the work, one contemplates all the inner and outer realms entirely as empty and still, preserving only the single mind, standing alone and unique. Therefore the ancients say: “Not to be companion to the ten thousand dharmas, not to be counterpart to the various dusts.” If the mind attaches to the realm, the mind is precisely the false mind; now that there is no realm, how can there be falsehood? It is the true mind alone shining, unimpeded in the Way, which is the ancients' approach of seizing the realm and not the person. Hence the saying: “The flowers of the upper garden have fallen; the carriages and horses are still thronging.” And again: “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind.]

Fourth, extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind. When doing the work, one contemplates all the inner and outer realms completely as empty and still (“whatever has characteristics is all vain and false”), preserving only the single mind, standing alone and unique (not connecting with the inner and outer realms). Therefore the ancients say: “Not to be companion to the ten thousand dharmas, not to have any connection with the various dusts.” If the mind attaches to the realm, then the mind is the false mind; now that there is no realm, where could there be a false mind? This is the true mind alone shining, not impeding the Way, which is the ancients' approach of seizing the realm and not the mind. Hence the verse says: “The flowers of the upper garden (the imperial garden) have withered (extinguishing the realm); there are still many carriages and horses gathered (preserving the mind).” And again: “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the realm and preserving the mind.
[The carriages and horses still thronging (
pián tián

)] There are still many carriages and horses gathered there. [The three thousand swordsmen] Describing the world in great disorder, the many heroes contending (three thousand swordsmen), planning to pacify the world. [Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace] Reckoning it over, only Master Zhuang was lofty, transcending the world and departing from the common (the mind not seizing the realm, the realm naturally extinguished), enjoying peace.
However, the allusion of “Where are the three thousand swordsmen today? Only reckoning on Zhuang Zhou was there peace” comes from the Zhuangzi
Miscellaneous Chapters

On Swords: King Wen of Zhao was so fond of swordsmanship that he spent all day with swordsmen and neglected the government of the state. Swashbucklers surged in, more than three thousand in number. They competed day and night in swordsmanship, and every year over a hundred were killed or wounded. This went on for three years, the state's strength waned day by day, and the lords of the various states were all plotting how to attack Zhao. The crown prince was deeply worried and invited Master Zhuang to go and persuade him. Zhuang Zhou said to King Wen of Zhao: “There are three kinds of swords, namely the sword of the Son of Heaven, the sword of the feudal lords, and the sword of the common people. Now the Great King holds the position of one who wins the world, yet delights in the sword of the common people; I privately deeply despise this for the Great King, and hope the Great King will grasp the sword of the Son of Heaven.” So King Wen of Zhao reflected deeply, and for three months did not leave his palace gate to watch swordsmanship. The three thousand swordsmen, losing favor and ashamed and angry, would not live dishonorably, and all killed themselves at their lodgings.

blocks.text: 5. Extinguishing the Mind and Extinguishing the Realm

inline.s: [Fifth, extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm. It means that when doing the work, one first empties the external realm, then extinguishes the inner mind. Since both inner mind and outer realm are still, how after all can delusion exist? Hence Guanxi says: “In the ten directions there is no wall; on the four sides there is also no gate; naked, utterly bare.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing both person and realm. Hence the saying: “The clouds scatter and the water flows away; still and silent, heaven and earth are empty.” And again: “Neither the person nor the ox is seen; it is exactly the time of the bright moon.” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm.]

Fifth, extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm. When doing the work, one first empties the external realm, and then extinguishes the inner mind. Since both inner mind and outer realm are still, after all from whence can delusion come? Hence the Master Guanxi says: “In the ten directions there are no windows (walls); on the four sides there is also no gate; naked (utterly bare), utterly bare.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing both mind and realm. Hence the verse says: “The clouds scatter and the water flows away; still and silent, heaven and earth are empty.” And again: “Neither the person (the cowherd) nor the ox (the ox he tends) is seen; it is exactly the time of the bright moon (the true mind shining alone).” This is the stilling work of extinguishing the mind and extinguishing the realm.

blocks.text: 6. Preserving the Realm and Preserving the Mind

inline.s: [Sixth, preserving the realm and preserving the mind. It means that when doing the work, the mind abides in the position of mind, the realm abides in the position of realm. Sometimes when mind and realm confront each other, then the mind does not seize the realm, and the realm does not approach the mind; each not reaching the other, naturally false thoughts do not arise, and there is no hindrance to the Way. Hence the sutra says: “This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing neither person nor realm. Hence the saying: “A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?” And again: “Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return.” This is the work of extinguishing delusion by preserving the realm and preserving the mind.]

Sixth, preserving the realm and preserving the mind. When doing the work, the mind abides in the position of mind, the realm abides in the position of realm. When mind and realm confront each other, then the mind does not seize the realm and the realm does not enter the mind; each not reaching the other (the mind and realm unhook), naturally false thoughts do not arise, and there is no hindrance to the practice of the Way. Hence the Lotus Sutra says: “This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent.” This is the patriarchs' approach of seizing neither mind nor realm. Hence the verse says: “A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?” And again: “Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return.” This is the work of extinguishing delusion by preserving the realm and preserving the mind.

[Each not reaching the other] The mind not seizing the realm, the realm not entering the mind; this is the “mind like a wall” that the Patriarch Bodhidharma transmitted to the Second Patriarch Huike. (For details see
The Detailed Explanation of the Treatise on the Two Entrances and Four Practices

) [This Dharma abides in the position of Dharma; the characteristics of the world are permanent] This Dharma, that is, should abide in the position of Dharma (not entering the mind); thus the characteristics of the world are the permanent true reality, that is, in the apparent arising and ceasing (the characteristics of the world), one sees only the unborn (true reality). This is what is meant by: “When the whole world praises him, he does not thereby rejoice; when the whole world blames him, he does not thereby be dejected; he is fixed in the distinction between inner and outer, clear about the realm of honor and disgrace.” (See the Zhuangzi, Wandering in the void.) Translation: When the whole society praises him, he is not therefore glad; when the whole society blames him, he is not therefore dejected. He can determine the boundary between the inner mind and outer realm, and clearly know that such outer realms as honor and disgrace are but illusions. (The “quan” in the line, used for “huan,” means joy. For example, the Hanfeizi, the Eight Villainies, says: “To please his mind and make him offend against his lord.”) [A single moon rises from the sea; how many families go upstairs?] The bright moon rising over the eastern sea, this is a beautiful scene, yet how many people go upstairs to enjoy it? This too is a metaphor for the realm and the mind, each not reaching the other, mutually unconcerned. [Mountain flowers in thousands of blossoms; the wandering son does not know to return] The mountain flowers in full bloom are a beautiful scene, yet the wandering son does not therefore return home to enjoy them. This too is a metaphor for the realm and the mind, each not reaching the other, mutually unconcerned.
